question:
In the figure, \(CD,\) \(AE,\) and \(BF\) are one-third of their respective sides. It follows that \(AN_2:N_2N_1:N_1D=3:3:1,\) and similarly for lines \(BE\) and \(CF.\) Then the area of triangle \(N_1N_2N_3\) is:

[Figure 1](figures/1952_AMC_12_Q49_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The supplied \(3:3:1\) divisions let us compare areas without finding any angles or side lengths. Write \([XYZ]\) for the area of triangle \(XYZ\), and let \(K=[ABC]>0\). Triangles with bases on the same line and a common opposite vertex have the same altitude, so their areas are proportional to their bases.

Since \(CD=\tfrac13BC\), we have \(BD=\tfrac23BC\), giving \([ABD]=\tfrac23K\). Also, the given division of \(AD\) gives
\[
\frac{AN_2}{AD}=\frac{3}{3+3+1}=\frac37.
\]
Using bases \(AN_2\) and \(AD\), with common opposite vertex \(B\), we obtain
\[
[ABN_2]=\frac37[ABD]
=\frac37\cdot\frac23K=\frac27K.
\]
The analogous divisions along \(BE\) and \(CF\) give \(BN_3/BE=3/7\) and \(CN_1/CF=3/7\). Since \(CE=\tfrac23CA\) and \(AF=\tfrac23AB\), the same shared-altitude reasoning gives
\[
[BCN_3]=\frac37[BCE]=\frac27K,
\]
\[
[CAN_1]=\frac37[CAF]=\frac27K.
\]
The three triangles \(ABN_2\), \(BCN_3\), and \(CAN_1\), together with the central triangle \(N_1N_2N_3\), fill \(ABC\). Their interiors do not overlap: the drawn segments \(AD\), \(BE\), and \(CF\) separate these regions. Therefore
\[
[N_1N_2N_3]
=K-3\left(\frac27K\right)
=\frac17K.
\]
The central triangle has \(\boxed{\tfrac17}\) of the area of \(ABC\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

edges.reason: Triangle classification helps recognize where an altitude may lie. The area relation and a supplied base/height can be used across all triangle types without first sorting them as acute, right or obtuse.
edges.scope: locating heights in right and obtuse triangles

edges.reason: The target explicitly states that the triangle has half the area of an equal-base equal-height parallelogram. Parallelogram-area meaning is needed for that specified comparison.

The criterion explicitly permits triangles OR rectangles. Both external reviews turn that alternative into an unconditional requirement, but an L-shaped orthogonal figure can be split entirely into rectangles. Preserve triangle area as a component of the triangular-piece route without making every composite-area task use it.
edges.scope: Calculating triangular pieces in a triangular partition of a composite area

edges.reason: The integer-multiplier case supplies a useful stepping stone and repeated-addition interpretation. The product-of-numerators/product-of-denominators rule follows directly from a part-of-a-part area model without executing the earlier decimal-free integer-multiplier procedure; Gemini confuses this customary progression with necessity.
Simplifying a ratio can reduce arithmetic. Sharing 60 in the ratio 4 to 6 by ten equal units already gives 24 and 36, so the greatest-common-factor simplification procedure is optional preparation.

Both the unit-part and fraction-of-total methods read the given ratio as relative shares. Simplifying to lowest terms is optional, whereas this meaning is common to the methods. Root checked both endpoint-based reviews; each identifies the stated content or conditional method rather than a curriculum-order claim.
edges.scope: Understanding the ratio terms as relative part counts before allocating a total
